absent: Internals of common timer and sleep helpers referenced by the clock bundles
Definitions and behavior of process, thread, alarm and auxiliary clock bundles
Timer identifier allocation, hash lookup, signal delivery and permission checks
Base jiffy timeout engine, signal pending test and task wakeup mechanics
Hrtimer sleeper structure and hrtimer core start, cancel and forward semantics
Clocksource multiplier, shift and wrap limit calculation helpers
Interrupt time accounting enablement effects and policy beyond the rate threshold
Tick broadcast lock, tick device layout, handler installation and idle interaction
Syscore registration lifecycle and suspend ordering guarantees
Debugfs file operation helpers and sequence file iteration mechanics
Coarse and raw time read sources and resolution values
Concurrency checker marking and preemption control internals

findings.text: The time subsystem exposes a dispatch table indexed by clock identifier that resolves each supported clock to a dedicated operation bundle. Coverage seen includes realtime, monotonic, processor and thread processor time, raw monotonic, coarse realtime and coarse monotonic, boottime, two alarm clocks sharing one bundle, TAI, and an optional auxiliary range. Callers select behavior by identifier rather than branching on clock kind.

Clock behavior is factored into a single operation bundle type. It groups resolution query, wall setting and adjustment, two read forms distinguished by time namespace scope, a sleep entry, and a timer family covering creation, configuration, query, deletion, rearming, forwarding overruns, remaining query, cancellation attempt, arming and waiting for a running instance. Clocks populate only the subset they support.

Capability split is stable across the shown clocks. Full timer plus sleep support appears on realtime, monotonic, boottime and TAI, while raw and coarse variants expose only resolution and current time reads. Among the shown instances only realtime implements setting and adjustment. Monotonic family sleeps use a namespace aware variant whereas realtime and TAI use the common variant.

Posix timer lifecycle uses three logical states: disarmed, armed, and a requeue pending marker used when expiry handling must be retried. Transitions move from disarmed to armed on successful arming and back on deletion or expiry without reload, with the pending marker as an intermediate when requeue cannot complete immediately.
TIMER_RETRY denotes numeric value one.

Early initialization prepares posix timer storage by creating a dedicated slab cache for timer objects and allocating a large hashed bucket array sized from processor count with a small system fallback. It derives a mask from the power of two size and initializes each bucket for later hashing.

Each hash bucket carries its own spinlock guarding its chain. Locks are initialized once during early setup before any timer can be hashed, giving fine grained protection per bucket rather than a single global lock.

Scheduler clock state centers on a cache aligned record holding a latch sequencer, two copies of read parameters, a wrap interval, a rate estimate, and the active low level counter reader. Readers select a copy by sequence parity while writers publish through the latch.

Time reads combine an epoch base with masked delta from a counter converted by multiply and shift. Readers sample the latch, compute from the selected copy, and retry if the writer moved. External begin and retry helpers expose the same parity selection for outside users, and the early fallback derives ticks from jiffies.

Two scheduler clock read entries exist with identical time computation but different context handling. One is usable in instrumented context and briefly blocks preemption while marking the region atomic for the concurrency checker. The other is explicitly non instrumented for use where probing is forbidden.

Publication to scheduler clock readers follows a latch discipline that first steers readers to the spare copy, then refreshes the main copy, flips readers back, refreshes the spare, and closes the sequence. This lets lock free readers always see a consistent parameter set without blocking.

Epoch maintenance advances the base time to the current counter value using the active conversion, preserving continuity across updates. A periodic callback performs this refresh and then schedules itself again after the precomputed wrap interval so the counter never wraps unnoticed.

Registration of a scheduler clock source rejects sources slower than the current one, requires local interrupts to be held, derives conversion and wrap limits from rate and width, carries time forward from the old counter to the new epoch, publishes the new parameters, restarts the wrap timer when already running, and enables interrupt time accounting when the rate is fast enough or explicitly requested.

Generic initialization guarantees a usable scheduler clock even when no platform source registered by installing the jiffy based fallback, refreshing the epoch once, and starting a monotonic hard relative wrap timer that keeps the epoch current.

Suspend and resume form a frozen versus live pair. Suspend refreshes the epoch, stops the wrap timer, and swaps reads to a frozen accessor returning the saved epoch counter. Resume recaptures the live counter, restarts the wrap timer, and restores the live accessor. System core hooks wire these transitions into platform suspend and resume.
Blocking timeout state pairs a standard timer list node with the task to be woken. Expiry simply wakes that task, letting the sleeper return through the normal scheduler path.
Killable and idle sleep helpers set the current task state to the respective killable or idle flavor and then delegate to the generic jiffy based timeout wait, returning its remaining count.

High resolution bounded sleep takes an expiry, a slack window, a mode and a clock choice. Zero expiry succeeds immediately without waiting, a missing expiry waits indefinitely and reports interruption, otherwise a stacked sleeper is armed over the requested range, the caller blocks while still owning the sleeper, then the timer is cancelled and torn down with success versus interruption decided by continued ownership.
Two thin wrappers fix common choices for the range sleep: one defaults the clock to monotonic while preserving slack and mode, the other further fixes slack to zero while preserving expiry and mode.
Interruptible millisecond sleep converts the request to jiffies and repeatedly waits while time remains and no signal is pending, finally reporting the leftover converted back to milliseconds.

Microsecond range sleep builds an absolute deadline from now plus the minimum and derives tolerance from the width of the requested interval. An inverted range collapses tolerance to zero with a one time warning. It then repeatedly marks the requested state and waits absolute until the deadline has elapsed.
DEFAULT_ITERATIONS denotes numeric value one hundred.
DEBUGFS_FILENAME denotes the short name udelay_test.

A dedicated mutex serializes access to the delay test configuration and debug file lifetime. Both the display and update paths sample or store settings under this lock, and creation and removal of the debug entry also hold it.

The delay test exposes a debug file whose read either runs a measurement batch when configured or prints usage plus current loop and time parameters when idle, while writes accept a microsecond count with optional iteration count defaulting when omitted and reject overlong or unparsable input.

Delay measurement tolerates a small fast error proportional to the request, tracks minimum, average and maximum elapsed as well as a failure count for samples below the adjusted expectation, and warns if time appears to go backwards. Results are formatted as a single summary line with an optional failure suffix.

The broadcast fallback device is allowed on any possible processor, carries zero rating with initially unbound placement, uses identity conversion, accepts an extreme delta span from one unit to the maximum, advertises one shot plus hrtimer capability, and presents itself under a short hrtimer name.

Broadcast shutdown and reprogramming must never block waiting for the callback because the broadcast lock is already held on entry and the callback itself needs that lock, creating a deadlock, with the handler additionally unable to wait for itself. Arming always targets the local processor but stays put when the callback is running, and the recorded binding is refreshed from the timer base while still under the broadcast lock.

Broadcast setup initializes the shared hrtimer for monotonic absolute hard expiry with a handler that simply forwards to the registered device callback and requests no restart, then registers the fallback device with the clock events core.
Broadcast bookkeeping keeps a central tick device, two persistent masks plus a scratch mask for set operations, a forced flag, and a per processor pointer to the wakeup clock device.
Two accessors expose broadcast state: one returns the mask of processors using broadcast, the other returns the wakeup device assigned to a given processor.

Reception of a broadcast on the current processor looks up its tick device and invokes the installed handler. A missing device reports ENODEV and a missing handler reports EINVAL, otherwise success is reported after the handler runs.
Oneshot wakeup handling first clears the forced marker on the wakeup device and then performs normal broadcast reception. Early or reprogrammed wakeups are accepted as harmless spurious events.
